```{r setup}
library(diseasy)
```

```{r hidden_options, include = FALSE}
withr::local_options("diseasystore.verbose" = FALSE)
withr::local_options("tibble.print_min" = 5)
```

# Overview

The `DiseasyPopulation` module is responsible for defining the model population and interfacing with the models.

Presently, `DiseasyPopulation` combines `DiseasyRegions` and `DiseasyActivity` to configure a model population
stratified by age and geographical region. Where `DiseasyRegions` defines the _scope_ and possible stratifications of
the model population, `DiseasyPopulation` manages the stratification itself. Similarly, `DiseasyActivity` defines the
age-specific interactions between age groups as well as age-specific societal restrictions over time,
while `DiseasyPopulation` aggregates these effects into user stratified age groups.
Combined, this forms a model population stratified both spatially and by age groups.

# Defining the population of interest

The first step of defining the model population is to define a population of interest.

For `DiseasyPopulation`, this is done via `DiseasyRegions`[^1] which handles demography data
(see `vignette(diseasy-regions)` for more details).

[^1]: Or, as in this case, `DiseasyRegionsNuts` which is a generalisation of `DiseasyRegions`.

```{r regions}
regions <- DiseasyRegionsNuts$new(
  demography = demography_nordic_nuts3, # Use demography data from EUROSTAT
  adjacency = adjacency_meta_nordic_nuts3, # Use adjacency data from Meta
  area = "DK" # Restrict population of interest to Danish population
)

regions
```

Once the scope of the population has been defined in `DiseasyRegions`, this can be passed to
`DiseasyPopulation` to handle the remaining configuration of the model population.

```{r load-regions}
population <- DiseasyPopulation$new(regions = regions)

population
```

# Defining the age-specific interactions

If the model population should be stratified by age, the next step is to
configure the age-specific interactions between age groups (contact matrices).
In `diseasy`, this is done via the `DiseasyActivity`[^2].

[^2]: `DiseasyActivity` also defines (age-specific) changes in societal restrictions
if needed for the model -- but this is not done for this example.

```{r activity}
activity <- DiseasyActivity$new(
  contact_basis = contact_basis_nordic %.% DK
)

activity
```

... and, once a basis of contact matrices has defined, the `DiseasyActivity`
can be passed to `DiseasyPopulation`.

```{r load-activity}
population$load_module(activity)

population
```

# Stratifying to form the model population

With the population basis defined via `DiseasyRegions` and `DiseasyActivity`,
the model population can now be stratified at various resolutions to before
being passed to the models.

To stratify by age, we use the `?DiseasyPopulation$stratify_age()` method:
```{r stratify-age}
population$stratify_age(age_cuts_lower = c(0, 20, 40, 60, 80))

# and we can inspect the defined demographic groups
population$model_population
```

To stratify by region, we use the `?DiseasyPopulation$stratify_regions()` method:
```{r stratify-regions}
population$stratify_regions(regional_stratification = "NUTS 2")

# .. and we can inspect the updated demographic groups
population$model_population
```

# Populations outside the Nordics

To keep the installation size of `diseasy` light, we only bundle population data
for the Nordic countries.

To generate data for other regions, see the data generating functions:
`generate_demography()`, `generate_contact_basis()`, etc.



# Notes: Regional aggregation of contact matrices

The source data for the contact matrices we use in `diseasy` is typically collections of survey data where
participants have been instructed to count contacts with other individuals along with the approximate age of
these individuals. These survey data are then corrected for differences in demography of the participants
and the group they are meant to represent (e.g. a given country) to form a "full" contact matrix for the
target population.


```{r, include = FALSE, eval = rlang::is_installed("igraph")}
# Define some helper functions

# A plotter for the adjacency graphs
adjacency_graph <- function(adjacency) {
  graph <- igraph::graph_from_adjacency_matrix(
    adjmatrix = adjacency,
    mode = "undirected",
    diag = FALSE
  )

  region <- stringr::str_extract(population$group, r"{\w+$}")
  age <- stringr::str_extract(population$group, r"{^\w+}")

  layout <- cbind(
    x = as.numeric(factor(region)),
    y = as.numeric(factor(age))
  )

  # Add some jitter so vertices in the same region/age group do not overlap
  layout <- layout + matrix(
    stats::runif(length(layout), -0.3, 0.3),
    ncol = 2
  )

  plot(
    graph,
    layout = layout,
    vertex.color = factor(region),
    vertex.shape = "circle",
    vertex.label = population$group,
    vertex.size = 30
  )
}
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
# A method for aggregating data (typically adjacency) in new sub groups
aggregate_contacts <- function(adjacency, population, groups) {

  p <- purrr::map(
    unique(groups),
    ~ as.numeric(groups == .x)
  ) |>
    purrr::reduce(
      rbind,
      .init = matrix(0, nrow = 0, ncol = length(population))
    )

  # Count population by group
  n_groups <- lengths(split(groups, factor(groups)))[unique(groups)]

  colnames(p) <- population
  rownames(p) <- paste0(names(n_groups), " (", n_groups, ")")

  return(p %*% adjacency %*% t(p))
}

# A printing function which uses dots (...) to print wide and long matrices
print_truncated <- function(x, n = 3) {
  nr <- nrow(x)
  nc <- ncol(x)

  rows <- unique(c(seq_len(min(n, nr)), seq.int(max(nr - n + 1, 1), nr)))
  cols <- unique(c(seq_len(min(n, nc)), seq.int(max(nc - n + 1, 1), nc)))

  y <- format(x[rows, cols, drop = FALSE])

  if (nr > 2 * n)
    y <- rbind(
      y[seq_len(n), , drop = FALSE],
      "...",
      y[(n + 1):(2 * n), , drop = FALSE]
    )

  if (nc > 2 * n)
    y <- cbind(
      y[, seq_len(n), drop = FALSE],
      "...",
      y[, (n + 1):(2 * n), drop = FALSE]
    )

  print(y, quote = FALSE)
}
```


To gain some intuition on the how these contact matrices can be interpreted and manipulated we will
begin by considering some toy-examples with a toy population of age groups ("A", "B", "C") and spatial
regions ("x", "y", "z", "w").

```{r}
population <- tibble::tibble(
  "group" = c(
    rep("A/x", 3), rep("B/x", 2), rep("C/x", 1),
    rep("A/y", 1), rep("B/y", 2), rep("C/y", 3),
    rep("A/z", 1), rep("B/z", 1), rep("C/z", 1),
    rep("A/w", 1), rep("B/w", 2), rep("C/w", 1)
  )
) |> tidyr::separate_wider_delim(
  cols = "group", delim = "/", names = c("age_group", "region"), cols_remove = FALSE
)
age_groups <- unique(population$age_group)
regions <- unique(population$region)

# Store as factors
population <- population |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    "age_group" = factor(.data$age_group, levels = age_groups),
    "region" = factor(.data$region, levels = regions),
    "group" = factor(.data$group, levels = unique(.data$group))
  )

table(population$group)
```

Assuming age-specific total contacts ("T" domain - see `vignette("diseasy-activity")` for more details):
```{r}
N_age <- stats::xtabs(~ age_group, data = population)

t_matrix <- round(
  outer(
    1.5 / seq_along(age_groups),
    1.5 / seq_along(age_groups)
  )^1.25 * N_age %*% t(N_age)
)

print(t_matrix)
```

... and age-specific mean contact rates ("M" domain) of:
```{r}
m_matrix <- t_matrix / outer(rep(1, length(N_age)), N_age)
print(round(m_matrix, digits = 2))
```

.. and corresponding per-capita contact rates ("C" domain) of:
```{r}
c_matrix <- t_matrix / N_age %*% t(N_age)
print(round(c_matrix, digits = 2))
```

## A well-mixed example

Consider the well-mixed case where a population of individuals across different age groups and
spatial locations are equally likely to be connected.

We can draw a realisation of such a network from our contact matrices
<details>
  <summary>See implementation</summary>

```{r}
# Convert T-matrix to long-form data.frame
one_way_links <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  i_age_group = age_groups,
  j_age_group = age_groups
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    "n_contacts" = as.vector(t_matrix)
  ) |>
  tidyr::uncount(.data$n_contacts) |>
  dplyr::select(!"n_contacts")

# Randomly draw i indices (from nodes)
one_way_links <- one_way_links |>
  dplyr::group_by(.data$i_age_group) |>
  dplyr::group_modify(
    ~ .x |>
      dplyr::mutate(
        "i" = sample(
          x = which(
            stringr::str_starts(population$group, .y$i_age_group)
          ),
          size = dplyr::n(),
          replace = TRUE
        )
      )
  )

# Randomly draw j indices (to nodes)
one_way_links <- one_way_links |>
  dplyr::group_by(.data$i, .data$j_age_group) |>
  dplyr::group_modify(
    ~ .x |>
      dplyr::mutate(
        "j" = sample(
          x = which(
            stringr::str_starts(population$group, .y$j_age_group) &
              seq_along(population$group) != .y$i
          ),
          size = dplyr::n(),
          replace = TRUE
        )
      )
  )

# Finalise
one_way_links <- one_way_links |>
  dplyr::mutate( # Make lower
    "i_u" = pmax(.data$i, .data$j),
    "j_u" = pmin(.data$i, .data$j)
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(.data$i_u, .data$j_u) |>
  dplyr::summarise("n" = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") # Count connections

# Convert to adjacency matrix with 2-way interactions
adjacency_sw <- as.matrix(
  Matrix::sparseMatrix(
    i = one_way_links$i_u,
    j = one_way_links$j_u,
    x = one_way_links$n,
    dims = c(nrow(population), nrow(population)),
    dimnames = list(population$group, population$group)
  )
)

# Make symmetric
adjacency_sw <- (adjacency_sw + t(adjacency_sw)) / 2

print_truncated(adjacency_sw)
```
</details>

```{r, eval = rlang::is_installed("igraph")}
adjacency_graph(adjacency_sw)
```

From this full adjacency graph, we can project the contacts ("T" domain) into contact matrices in different stratifications.

Number of contacts stratified by age group and region (with population size in parentheses):
```{r}
T_age_region <- aggregate_contacts(
  adjacency = adjacency_sw,
  population = population$group,
  groups = population$group # No aggregation
)

print_truncated(T_age_region)
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(T_age_region))
```

Stratify only by region:
```{r}
T_region <- aggregate_contacts(
  adjacency = adjacency_sw,
  population = population$group,
  groups = population$region
)

print(T_region)
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(T_region))
```

Stratify only by age group (and compare with input used to generate the adjacency graph)
```{r}
T_age <- aggregate_contacts(
  adjacency = adjacency_sw,
  population = population$group,
  groups = population$age_group
)

print(T_age)
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(T_age))

# Reference
print(t_matrix)
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(t_matrix))
```

Let's see if we can achieve these same contacts without explicitly generating the network.

First, the mixing matrix for well-mixed scenario is:
```{r}
mixing_sw <- matrix(
  data = 1,
  nrow = length(regions),
  ncol = length(regions),
  dimnames = list(regions, regions)
)
print(mixing_sw)
```

Notice that we now have a population stratified by age in age groups $i$ and $j$,
and a regional mixing matrix connecting regions $x$ and $y$.
The population is therefore currently identified by the simultaneous indices ($i, x$),
which we combine to form a linear "demography group" index connecting individuals
from demographic groups $q$ and $p$.
So that $p$ and $q$ enumerate all combinations of age and region ($i, x$).

The models population is expressed in this linear index and, therefore, we aim to
combine the regional mixing and age-specific matrices into a single representation
in the linear demography group indices. A "full" rather than "marginal" contact
matrix.

We can compute the "full" per-capita contact matrix, $\overline{\overline{C}}^{\textrm{full}}$,
from the age-specific contact matrix, $\overline{\overline{C}}$,
the regional mixing matrix, $\overline{\overline{\Theta}}$,
and the population vector, $\overline{N}$ with indices $p = (i, x)$: via the elementwise relation:
$$
C^{\textrm{full}}_{p = (i, x), q = (j, y)} = k_{i, j} C_{i, j} \Theta^\ast_{x, y}
$$

Where $k_{i,j}$ is a age-group normalisation (see below) and $\overline{\overline{\Theta^\ast}}$
is a normalised mixing matrix between regions:
$$
\overline{\overline{\Theta^\ast}} = \frac{\overline{\overline{\Theta}}}{\overline{n}^T\overline{\overline{\Theta}}\overline{n}}
$$

with $\overline{n}$ being the population fraction:
$$
\overline{n} = \frac{\overline{N}}{\overline{1}^T\overline{N}}
$$

The normalisation $\overline{n}^T\overline{\overline{\Theta}}\overline{n}$ is the *population-pair-weighted* average
of the entries of $\Theta$.



The normalized entry $\Theta^{\ast}_{ij}$ is a relative contact multiplier:
For example,

$$
\Theta^\ast_{x,y} = 1.4
$$

means that contacts between regions $x$ and $y$ are multiplied by 1.4, relative to the average mixing effect.

Note that the normalization preserves the population-pair-weighted regional mixing intensity.
Consequently, the total number of contacts is invariant only when regional age compositions are identical.

This is where the additional normalisation constants $k_{i, j}$ comes in.

We first define mixing-weighted population-pair volume $D_{i,j}$ as:

$$
D_{i,j} = \sum_{x,y} \Theta^\ast_{x,y} N_{i,x} N_{j,y}.
$$

That is, the number of potential population pairs between age groups $i$ and $j$
when accounting for the mixing between regions.

The additional normalisation then becomes:
$$
k_{i, j} = \frac{ \sum_x N_{i,x} \sum_x N_{j,x}}{D_{i,j}}
$$

which preserves the age-specific contact volume when aggregating across the regions.


Let's see that computation in practice:
```{r}
N_age_region <- stats::xtabs(~ age_group + region, data = population)

print(N_age_region)
```

```{r}
N_region <- stats::xtabs(~ region, data = population)
n_region <- N_region / sum(N_region)

print(n_region)
```

```{r}
theta <- mixing_sw

theta_norm <- theta / drop(t(n_region) %*% theta %*% n_region)
k <- N_age %*% t(N_age) / (N_age_region %*% theta_norm %*% t(N_age_region))

c_matrix_full_sw <- kronecker(theta_norm, c_matrix * k)
dimnames(c_matrix_full_sw) <- list(
  unique(population$group),
  unique(population$group)
)
print_truncated(round(c_matrix_full_sw, digits = 1))
```

The per-capita contact matrix can then be cast to the number of contacts ("T" domain).
```{r}
N <- as.matrix(table(population$group))

t_matrix_full_sw <- c_matrix_full_sw * tcrossprod(N)
print_truncated(round(t_matrix_full_sw, digits = 1))
```

Finally, we can aggregate the raw contact matrix in the same groups as the original reference (i.e. age groups only) and compare with that reference.
```{r}
T_age_indirect <- aggregate_contacts(
  t_matrix_full_sw,
  population = unique(population$group),
  groups = unique(population$age_group)
)

print_truncated(round(T_age_indirect, digits = 1))
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(T_age_indirect))

# Reference
print(t_matrix)
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(t_matrix))
```

## A silo example
Consider a complementary network where a population of individuals across different age groups and
spatial locations are well-mixed only within their spatial region (an extremely "siloed" network).

We can draw a realisation of such a network from our contact matrices
<details>
  <summary>See implementation</summary>

```{r}
# Convert T matrix to long-form data.frame
one_way_links <- tidyr::expand_grid(
  i_age_group = age_groups,
  j_age_group = age_groups
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    "n_contacts" = as.vector(t_matrix)
  ) |>
  tidyr::uncount(.data$n_contacts) |>
  dplyr::select(!"n_contacts")

# Randomly draw i indices (from nodes)
# verify they connect to j nodes in the region
# -- else re-draw from accepted samples
one_way_links <- one_way_links |>
  dplyr::group_by(.data$i_age_group) |>
  dplyr::group_modify(
    ~ {
      i_sampled <- .x |>
        dplyr::mutate(
          "i_age_group" = .y$i_age_group,
          "i" = sample(
            x = which(
              stringr::str_detect(population$group, .y$i_age_group)
            ),
            size = dplyr::n(),
            replace = TRUE
          ),
          "i_lab" = population$group[.data$i],
          "i_region" = stringr::str_extract(.data$i_lab, "[a-z]")
        )

      # Determine reachable connections
      i_sampled <- i_sampled |>
        dplyr::mutate(
          "any_j_reachable" = purrr::pmap_lgl(
            dplyr::select(i_sampled, "j_age_group", "i_region", "i"),
            \(j_age_group, i_region, i) {
              any(
                stringr::str_detect(
                  population$group,
                  stringr::str_replace(j_age_group, stringr::fixed("*"), i_region)
                ) & seq_along(population$group) != i
              )
            }
          )
        )

      # Determine reachable connections
      i_accepted <- i_sampled |>
        dplyr::filter(.data$any_j_reachable)

      # Re-sample unreachable from reachable
      i_resampled <- i_sampled |>
        dplyr::filter(!.data$any_j_reachable) |>
        dplyr::count(.data$i_age_group, .data$j_age_group) |>
        purrr::pmap(
          \(i_age_group, j_age_group, n) {
            i_accepted |>
              dplyr::filter(
                .data$i_age_group == {{ i_age_group }},
                .data$j_age_group == {{ j_age_group }}
              ) |>
              dplyr::slice_sample(n = {{ n }})
          }
        ) |>
        purrr::list_rbind()

      return(dplyr::select(rbind(i_accepted, i_resampled), !"i_age_group"))
    }
  )

# Randomly draw j indices (to nodes) within the same region
one_way_links <- one_way_links |>
  dplyr::group_by(.data$i, .data$j_age_group, .data$i_region) |>
  dplyr::group_modify(
    ~ .x |>
      dplyr::mutate(
        "j" = sample(
          x = which(
            stringr::str_detect(
              population$group,
              stringr::str_replace(
                .y$j_age_group,
                stringr::fixed("*"),
                .y$i_region
              )
            ) & seq_along(population$group) != .y$i
          ),
          size = dplyr::n(),
          replace = TRUE
        ),
        "j_lab" = population$group[.data$j],
        "j_region" = stringr::str_extract(.data$j_lab, "[a-z]")
      )
  )

# Finalise
one_way_links <- one_way_links |>
  dplyr::mutate( # Make lower
    "i_u" = pmax(.data$i, .data$j),
    "j_u" = pmin(.data$i, .data$j)
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(.data$i_u, .data$j_u) |>
  dplyr::summarise("n" = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") # Count connections

# Convert to adjacency matrix with 2-way interactions
adjacency_silo <- as.matrix(
  Matrix::sparseMatrix(
    i = one_way_links$i_u,
    j = one_way_links$j_u,
    x = one_way_links$n,
    dims = c(nrow(population), nrow(population)),
    dimnames = list(population$group, population$group)
  )
)

adjacency_silo <- (adjacency_silo + t(adjacency_silo)) / 2

print_truncated(adjacency_silo)
```
</details>

```{r, eval = rlang::is_installed("igraph")}
adjacency_graph(adjacency_silo)
```


Number of contacts stratified by age group and region
```{r}
T_age_region <- aggregate_contacts(
  adjacency = adjacency_silo,
  population = population$group,
  groups = population$group # No aggregation
)

print_truncated(T_age_region)
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(T_age_region))
```

Stratify only by region
```{r}
T_region <- aggregate_contacts(
  adjacency = adjacency_silo,
  population = population$group,
  groups = stringr::str_replace(population$group, r"{[A-Z]}", "*")
)

print(T_region)
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(T_region))
```

Stratify only by age group
```{r}
T_age <- aggregate_contacts(
  adjacency = adjacency_silo,
  population = population$group,
  groups = stringr::str_replace(population$group, r"{[a-z]}", "*")
)

print(T_age)
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(T_age))

# Reference
print(t_matrix)
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(t_matrix))
```


Again, Let's see if we can achieve these same contacts without generating the network.

```{r}
mixing_silo <- diag(
  x = 1,
  nrow = length(regions),
  ncol = length(regions)
)
dimnames(mixing_silo) <- list(regions, regions)
print(mixing_silo)
```


```{r}
theta <- mixing_silo

theta_norm <- theta / drop(t(n_region) %*% theta %*% n_region)
k <- N_age %*% t(N_age) / (N_age_region %*% theta_norm %*% t(N_age_region))

c_matrix_full_silo <- kronecker(theta_norm, c_matrix * k)
dimnames(c_matrix_full_silo) <- list(
  unique(population$group),
  unique(population$group)
)
print_truncated(round(c_matrix_full_silo, digits = 1))
```

```{r}
t_matrix_full_silo <- c_matrix_full_silo * tcrossprod(N)
print_truncated(round(t_matrix_full_silo, digits = 1))
```

```{r}
T_age_indirect <- aggregate_contacts(
  t_matrix_full_silo,
  population = unique(population$group),
  groups = unique(population$age_group)
)

print_truncated(round(T_age_indirect, digits = 1))
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(T_age_indirect))

# Reference
print(t_matrix)
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(t_matrix))
```

## A mixture example

Finally, Let's test the indirect method on a mixture of the two examples:

```{r}
mixing_mix <- matrix(
  data = 0.2,
  nrow = length(regions),
  ncol = length(regions)
) +
  diag(
    x = 0.8,
    nrow = length(regions),
    ncol = length(regions)
  )

dimnames(mixing_mix) <- list(regions, regions)
print(mixing_mix)
```


```{r}
theta <- mixing_mix

theta_norm <- theta / drop(t(n_region) %*% theta %*% n_region)
k <- N_age %*% t(N_age) / (N_age_region %*% theta_norm %*% t(N_age_region))

c_matrix_full_mix <- kronecker(theta_norm, c_matrix * k)
dimnames(c_matrix_full_mix) <- list(
  unique(population$group),
  unique(population$group)
)
print_truncated(round(c_matrix_full_mix, digits = 1))
```

```{r}
t_matrix_full_mix <- c_matrix_full_mix * tcrossprod(N)
print_truncated(round(t_matrix_full_mix, digits = 1))
```

```{r}
T_age_indirect <- aggregate_contacts(
  t_matrix_full_mix,
  population = unique(population$group),
  groups = unique(population$group)
)

print_truncated(round(T_age_indirect, digits = 1))
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(T_age_indirect))

# Reference
print(t_matrix)
cat("Total contacts: ", sum(t_matrix))
```

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
rm(
  regions,
  activity,
  population
)
gc()
```
